title: Nigerian jollof beats Ghanaian jollof (designed tie)
proposition: Nigerian jollof rice is better than Ghanaian jollof rice.
rationale: Mirror-image arguments of the same quality and length: each side names a preference criterion, describes its jollof accurately and concedes it is taste. Neither has a substantive edge, so the fair outcome is a draw (or inconclusive), not a forced winner.

opening.text: This is about taste, so here is my criterion: I want jollof where every grain carries the flavour of the stew. Nigerian jollof is usually made with long-grain parboiled rice, which stays firm and soaks up the tomato and pepper base evenly. Party jollof cooked over firewood adds a smoky flavour that many people love, and the slightly burnt bottom of the pot is a treat of its own.

rebuttal.text: Fragrant rice and shito are real strengths of Ghanaian jollof, and I understand why people love them. My preference is for the firmer grain and smoky depth of Nigerian jollof, but I accept that this comes down to what you enjoy.

opening.text: This is about taste, so here is my criterion: I want jollof where the rice itself has aroma as well as flavour. Ghanaian jollof is usually made with fragrant rice such as jasmine or basmati, which gives a lovely smell and a softer bite. It is often a little spicier, and served with shito, the pepper sauce, it has a depth of heat that many people love.

rebuttal.text: Firm parboiled grains and smoky party flavour are real strengths of Nigerian jollof, and I understand why people love them. My preference is for the aroma and heat of Ghanaian jollof, but I accept that this comes down to what you enjoy.
